problem: Existing outdoor navigation benchmarks (Touchdown, Map2Seq) use short routes, one or two cities, provide landmark or instruction annotations, and may be contaminated in MLLM pretraining. Raw MLLMs and reasoning techniques (CoT, reflection, GEPA) have not been tested on long-range, knowledge-intensive city navigation with no guidance.
motivation: Outdoor navigation needs self-localization, world knowledge, spatial reasoning and landmark recognition, which makes it a good probe of the knowledge stored in web-scale MLLMs. Prior embodied MLLM evaluations are mostly simulated, indoor, or language-centric. The paper observes that simply prompting the model to write out the destination address, its current location and walking directions elicits a latent city-scale cognitive map that greatly improves navigation.
key_idea: Prompt the MLLM at each intersection to verbalize the exact destination location, its current estimated location and walking directions between them (Verbalization of Path), combined with compact memory, to elicit internal city-scale world knowledge for zero-shot navigation.
insight: Most of the gain comes from grounding through verbalization, not from the memory. In the GPT-4.1 New York ablation the three memory components alone raise success from 15 to 35, Partial VoP (destination address only) gives 66, and full VoP gives 92. Generic reasoning scaffolds (CoT, reflection, GEPA, PReP, 7 engineered prompt variants at best 30 in NY) do not elicit this knowledge and degrade in long-horizon sequential settings. Failures come from non-Latin signage (Tokyo Kanji), which leads to loops, and from over-adherence to the initial plan.
method: Task formulation (Sparsely Grounded Visual Navigation): POMDP on a Street View graph; the agent sees only images of outgoing edges at each intersection, gets no landmarks, maps or instructions, and picks one street segment per step.

CityNav benchmark: 4 cities (New York, Tokyo, Vienna, Sao Paulo), 100 origin-destination pairs each, ~2 km routes with 44-80 decision points. Start points come from a crawler with a temperature-annealed softmax over heading and a revisit penalty. Destinations are manually drawn polygons. The Street View graph is preprocessed (dead-end pruning, reverse edges added, heading aligned by looking 3 nodes ahead).

Verbalization of Path (VoP): the prompt asks the agent to write the exact destination location, its current estimated exact location, and walking directions from current position to destination. Self-positioning is a separate MLLM call made every third decision point.
Markovian Memory: the model outputs a free-text memory state m_t that is fed back at the next step in place of the full episodic history (~100x less memory overhead).
Decision History: an ordered record of past actions at each intersection to avoid loops and support route correction.
Previous Visit tracking: per-node visit counts and prior decisions are shown to the agent, discouraging repeated actions at revisited intersections.

Evaluation platform and metrics: Success (reaching the destination polygon), SPL, and Decision Accuracy (the decision reduces remaining walking distance per the Google API). Budget is 150 decision points and 2000 node transitions.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 (thinking), O3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-32B (all frozen, prompted)
setting.observation: Google Street View 512x512 rectilinear crops (FOV 90, pitch +30) per outgoing edge at intersections, plus cardinal heading text; no visual input between intersections
setting.action_space: discrete choice among street-segment options at each intersection on the Street View graph
setting.simulator: Google Street View navigation graph (real-world imagery)
setting.privileged: none (destination name given; no landmarks, maps or GPS)

numbers_note: CityNav is the authors' own benchmark, so the bench names are 'other:'. Split is labeled 'test' by assumption because the paper mentions a 'test split' but gives no official split name. Success is reported as a percent of 100 episodes per city. Other model rows (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Gemini, Qwen) and baseline rows are in the tables but were not listed here. GPT-4.1 AgentNav in Tokyo, Vienna and Sao Paulo: 17/0.101/43.67, 32/0.182/49.95, 22/0.080/44.05.
results: VoP-based AgentNav improves success over the base model for every MLLM and city. GPT-4o in New York goes from 13 to 88, and GPT-4.1 from 15 to 92. O3 reaches 95 in NY and GPT-5 reaches 94. With GPT-4.1 it beats GEPA (37 in NY), PReP (39) and self-reflection (22), but non-NY cities remain hard (Tokyo 12-30, Sao Paulo 9-29 across models, e.g. GPT-5 30 in Tokyo).
limitations: Absolute success stays low in Tokyo, Vienna and Sao Paulo (especially with Kanji signage), with looping and over-reliance on the initial plan
Depends on Google Street View imagery and graph, which has residual inconsistencies; only 4 cities are covered, and the imagery cannot be released
Very strong performance in NY may reflect memorization of well-known city knowledge; the baselines are all evaluated on GPT-4.1 and the reported results have no variance
